title: How Sleep Paralysis Works, or The Worst Thing That Can Happen While You're Sleeping
summary: Josh and Chuck explain sleep paralysis: a state of consciousness with temporary inability to move or speak, usually accompanied by terror and vivid hallucinations (sense of presence, pressure on chest, sounds, smells, tastes). They cover the history of the word "nightmare" and the incubus, cultural interpretations (old hag in Newfoundland, ghost oppression in China, cookema in St. Lucia, kanashibari in Japan, witchcraft in European witch trials), links to alien abduction accounts, and the scientific explanation involving sleep onset REM periods, narcolepsy, and the amygdala. They discuss prevalence (roughly 3 to 6 percent isolated sleep paralysis, higher rates in narcolepsy and stress), how to break an episode by moving a small body part, false awakenings, and the harmlessness of the condition. The episode closes with a listener email from Tegan, a neuropsychology student in Melbourne.
topics: Stuff You Should Know listener mail

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction to sleep paralysis
segments.summary: Hosts open with a bit of stagecraft about sleep paralysis, joke about band names, and introduce the episode's definition of sleep paralysis from a British Psychological Society article. They note nightmare's original meaning and the incubus, and Josh shares his own exploding head experience and Chuck's great aunt with narcolepsy.

segments.title: Symptoms and fear of sleep paralysis
segments.summary: The hosts describe the experience: conscious but unable to move or speak, terror, a sense of presence, and auditory, visual, olfactory, gustatory and tactile hallucinations, including pressure on the chest. They discuss the role of fear, the amygdala, and how beliefs and pop culture shape the content of the episode.

segments.title: Cultural interpretations across history
segments.summary: The hosts survey how cultures explain sleep paralysis, including the old hag in Newfoundland, ghost oppression in China, spirit intrusion in anthropology, witchcraft accounts from European witch trials, cookema in St. Lucia, and kanashibari and similar terms in Japan and Korea.

segments.title: Alien abductions and historical accounts
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the link between sleep paralysis and UFO abduction accounts, including a study finding higher sleep paralysis rates among people who believe in abductions, and a fictional X-Files scene. They also mention Herman Melville's Moby Dick and Silas Weir Mitchell's early medical descriptions.

segments.title: Breaking an episode and its harmlessness
segments.summary: Advice on breaking sleep paralysis by moving a small body part or making a sound, and the fact that waking someone is safe. The hosts note that the condition is physiologically harmless and that learning this, and embracing the experience, can reduce its occurrence.

segments.title: Science: narcolepsy, sleep-onset REM and dual consciousness
segments.summary: The hosts explain the scientific basis: prevalence in narcolepsy (about 17 percent), isolated sleep paralysis in roughly 3 to 6 percent of people, severe and chronic forms, false awakenings, and the sleep-onset REM hypothesis. A Japanese study induced sleep-onset REM and found sleep paralysis in some participants. They describe REM atonia (cataplexy) and the brain being partly awake while still in REM.

segments.title: Treatment, prevention and closing thoughts
segments.summary: The hosts cover prevention through regular sleep schedules, treatment of narcolepsy with sodium oxybate, which does not reliably treat isolated sleep paralysis, and the recommendation to reframe the experience and reduce stress. They note the value of talking about it openly.

segments.title: Listener mail from Tegan
segments.summary: Tegan, a neuropsychology major in Melbourne, Australia, writes that the show helped her pass an exam and that her mother bought her a card. The hosts read the email and mention social media and contact info.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts sign off with contact information and the website reference.
